elements.sub: How living things get their fuel

elements.text: You ate lunch today. A neem tree outside did not eat anything. Yet both of you are alive and growing. How?
Carbon dioxide + water, powered by sunlight caught in chlorophyll, become glucose + oxygen
Gases enter and leave through tiny pores: stomata
The small intestine is where digested food is finally ABSORBED into the blood — through millions of finger-like villi
Plants trap energy from the sun; animals take it second-hand by eating. Either way, glucose is the fuel.

beats.narration: Here's a puzzle. You ate lunch today. The neem tree outside your window ate nothing — no lunch, no dinner, ever. Yet both of you are alive, growing, and full of energy. How does that work? That's what nutrition is about.

There are exactly two strategies for getting food. Autotrophs — plants and algae — build their own food from scratch. Heterotrophs — animals, fungi, and you — take it ready-made by eating others. Every living thing picks one of these two sides.

So how does a plant build food from scratch? Photosynthesis. Take carbon dioxide from the air, water from the soil, power it with sunlight trapped in chlorophyll — and out come glucose and oxygen. Read this equation carefully; it runs almost all life on Earth.

Picture the leaf as a factory. Carbon dioxide walks in through tiny pores called stomata, sunlight streams in from above, and oxygen walks out. Think about it — the oxygen you are breathing right now left a leaf through one of these pores.

Now your side of the story. Food enters the mouth, where chewing and saliva begin breaking it down. The stomach churns it with acid and enzymes. But here's the surprise — almost nothing enters your blood until the small intestine.

The small intestine is the real hero. Its wall is covered with millions of tiny finger-like projections called villi, which give it a huge surface area. That is where digested food is finally absorbed into your blood and delivered to every cell.

So, one line to remember: plants trap the sun's energy and build glucose; animals take that energy second-hand by eating. Either way, glucose is the fuel. And what does the body do with that fuel? That's our next lesson — respiration. Any doubts, raise your hand.
